Our evaluation answers the following three research questions:

RQ1: How effective is the PRP attack against Guard-Railed LLMs, when the adversary has white-box/black-box query access to the Guard Model?

RQ2: How well do the attacks generated by PRP transfer when the adversary has no access to the Guard Model?

RQ3: Do Guard Models offer any additional safety to the base aligned LLM?

RQ4: What is the trade-off between the individual components in PRP, i.e., finding a propagation prefix, and finding a universal adversarial prefix?

Datasets. We evaluate our attacks using prompts from Zou et al. (2023)'s Advbench dataset of harmful behavior prompts. This dataset contains 520 harmful prompts, out of which we select 100 for all our experiments except where stated otherwise. For PAP, we use the same set of harmful prompts as described in their paper (Zeng et al., 2024). LLMs. For $f_{LLM}$ , we consider several aligned and unaligned models. Aligned models include Llama2-70B-chat (Touvron et al., 2023), Vicuna-33B-v1.3 (Chiang et al., 2023), and Guanaco-13B (Dettmers et al., 2023). Unaligned models include Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 (Jiang et al., 2023), WizardLM-7B-Uncensored (Xu et al., 2023; Hartford, 2024a), and Wizard-LM-Falcon-7B-Uncensored (Almazrouei et al., 2023; Hartford, 2024b). For $g_{LLM}$ , we consider Llama2-70B-chat, Vicuna-33B-v1.3, LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023), OpenAI's gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 (OpenAI, 2023), and Google's Gemini-Pro (Anil et al., 2023) (latest models as available through respective APIs in February, 2024). Guard Model Configurations. We configure Guard Models with the template from Helbling et al. (2023): Does the following text contain harmful content: {response}. Respond with 'Yes, this is harmful' or 'No, this is not harmful'. A harmful response only evades the Guard Model when it outputs 'No'. We also consider a version of the much longer, alternative template used by LlamaGuard Algorithm 1 Universal Adversarial Prefix Input: Initial prefix $\delta_{\mathrm{init}}$ Guard Model LLM $g_{LLM}$ , maximum attack iterations max_aters, vocabulary token set $V$ , harmful responses set $R\subseteq V^{*}$ , number of new perturbation candidates $K$ for each index in the prefix, and threat model threat_model. Output: Perturbation $\delta$ s.t. $\mathbb{P}_{GLLM}(x_{\mathrm{No}}|\delta \cdot r) > 0.5\forall r\in R$ (success), else NULL (failure). 1: $\delta \gets \delta_{\mathrm{init}},\mathsf{n}\gets |\delta |$ Initialize universal adversarial prefix $\delta$ 2: for iter from 1 to max_aters do Attack loop to optimize prefix $\delta$ 3: candidates $=$ list( Initialize empty list of candidates for new prefix. 4: for i from 1 to n do Iterate over each index in the prefix $\delta$ 5: if threat_model $\equiv =$ black-box then 6: Pick $K$ new candidates by replacing $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ token in $\delta$ with random tokens. 7: $\delta_i^{\mathrm{cands}} = \mathrm{Substitute}_i^K (\delta ,\mathrm{Uniform})$ 8: else if threat_model $\equiv =$ white-box then 9: Pick $K$ new candidates by replacing $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ token in $\delta$ with tokens having largest gradients. 10: $\delta_i^{\mathrm{cands}} = \mathrm{Substitute}_i^K (\delta ,\mathrm{top}(\nabla_{x_i}\sum_{r\in R}[\mathbb{P}_{GLLM}(x_{\mathrm{No}}|\delta \cdot r)]))$ 11: end if 12: candidates extend $(\delta_i^{\mathrm{cands}})$ Add the $K$ new candidates to list. 13: end for 14: $\delta = \arg \max_{\delta \in \mathrm{candidates}}\left[\sum_{r\in R}[\mathbb{P}_{GLLM}(x_{\mathrm{No}}|\delta \cdot r)]\right]$ Select new $\delta$ from candidates list. 15: if $\mathbb{P}_{GLLM}(x_{\mathrm{No}}|\delta \cdot r) > 0.5\forall r\in R$ then Success if $\delta$ induces "No" via greedy sampling. 16: return $\delta$ 17: end if 18: end for 19: return NULL Failure if no $\delta$ can be found to induce "No". template provided in Appendix 3) which only looks at the response. Here, the decision tokens are instead 'unsafe' and 'safe'. Metrics. Our performance metric is attack success rate (ASR), which is the fraction of prompts for which we observe "attack success". For input prompt $p$ , the criterion for attack success is that Guard-Railed LLM $g_{(f_{LLM}, f_G)}$ returns a harmful response to $p$ , instead of refusal $(\perp)$ . To ensure that the returned response $f_{LLM}(p)$ is indeed harmful, we follow prior work (Zou et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2024), i.e., ensure it does not contain any refusal phrase from a pre-defined set of refusal phrases as a substring. We provide the list in Appendix A.1. PRP Configurations. We now describe our setup for generating prefixes for both stages of PRP: (a) Universal Adversarial Prefix. We generate 20 responses of length 100 tokens for optimization of the universal adversarial prefix using WizardLM-Vicuna-7B-Uncensored (Xu et al., 2023; Hartford, 2023). For any given Guard Model, we optimize over these 20 responses with a prefix of length 20 tokens (each initialized to '!'). In general we optimize for a maximum of 500 iterations, with $K = 256$ (Algorithm 1), and comparing 256 (white-box) * or 512 (black-box) candidates for updating the universal adversarial prefix. We find that this optimization is generally tractable — using 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, we are able to find a universal adversarial prefix for the largest Guard Model, i.e., Llama2-70B-chat within 70 minutes. When we do not even have white-box/black-box query access to the Guard Model LLM $g_{LLM}$ , we optimize over surrogate models in the hope that they transfer. We select 4 successful surrogate models from prior work (Zou et al., 2023) — Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B, Guanaco-7B, and Guanaco-13B. (a) Propagation Prefix. We construct propagation prefixes as a few-shot template using 10 or fewer input-output pairs as per Equation 6. For the input-output pairs, inputs are sampled either from AdvBench or the benign set of Kumar et al. (2023), with corresponding outputs generated by WizardLM-Vicuna-7B-Uncensored and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 respectively. Baselines. We consider baseline attacks from prior work, including GCG (Zou et al., 2023) and PAP (Zeng et al., 2024). NA stands for no attack applied.

Statement A.1. Given a Guard-Railed LLM $g_{(f_{LLM}, f_G)}$ and initial (potentially harmful) prompt $p_0$ such that $g_{(f_{LLM}, f_G)}(p_0) = \bot$ , the propagation prefix $p \to \Delta_{f_G}$ for the universal adversarial prefix $\Delta_{f_G}$ is a solution to the Guard-Rail Attack Problem in Equation 2. Proof. Using Equations 3 and 4, $$ \begin{array}{l} f _ {G} (f _ {L L M} (p _ {\rightarrow \Delta_ {f _ {G}}} \cdot p _ {0})) = f _ {G} (\Delta_ {f _ {G}} \cdot f _ {L L M} (p _ {0})) \\ = 0 \tag {7} \\ \end{array} $$ As per Equation 7, the Guard-Railed model always returns the LLM response, i.e., $$ \begin{array}{l} g _ {(f _ {L L M}, f _ {G})} (p _ {\rightarrow \Delta_ {f _ {G}}} \cdot p _ {0}) = f _ {L L M} (p _ {\rightarrow \Delta_ {f _ {G}}} \cdot p _ {0}) \\ = \Delta_ {f _ {G}} \cdot f _ {L L M} (p _ {0}) \tag {8} \\ \end{array} $$ ![](images/a029007d9d8ce768cc2bbe56b8be304973310247b551ae331dcb7d31bede112f.jpg) A.1 Refusal Phrases A.2 Additional Results
